title: The Proton Still Refuses to Die
hook: Super-Kamiokande searched its entire pure-water dataset for a proton decaying into a positron and something invisible. Nothing. The proton's lifetime in that channel now exceeds 1.7 x 10^33 years.
key_points: Grand unified theories generally predict the proton is unstable, though extremely long-lived.
This search targeted p -> l+ + X, where X is an invisible, massless, neutral particle.
It used 401 kiloton-years of exposure: the entire pure water phase of Super-Kamiokande.
No signal appeared above the expected atmospheric neutrino background.
Lower limits at 90% confidence: 1.72 x 10^33 years for the positron channel, 0.61 x 10^33 for the muon channel.
Those improve on previous limits by factors of about 2 and 1.5 respectively.
content_html: Nothing in the Standard Model makes the proton decay, but nearly every attempt to unify the forces does — at rates so slow that you need to watch an absurd number of protons to see one go. Super-Kamiokande, a 50,000-tonne tank of ultrapure water lined with photomultipliers, is how you watch that many.
extra_html: This search covers a channel where the proton decays into a single positively charged lepton plus X, an invisible massless neutral particle, using 401 kiloton-years of exposure — the entire pure water phase of the experiment. No candidate excess appeared beyond what atmospheric neutrinos are expected to produce. The resulting 90%-confidence lower limits on the partial lifetime are 1.72 x 10^33 years for decay to a positron and 0.61 x 10^33 years for decay to a muon, improving on previous bounds by factors of roughly 2 and 1.5. Null results like this are how the space of grand unified theories actually gets narrowed: each order of magnitude in lifetime kills off models that predicted faster decay.

related.title: The Standard Model
related.hook: Almost everything around you is built from a handful of particles obeying three forces — and one theory predicts it all with jaw-dropping precision, yet still can't explain gravity.

related.title: Catching the Ghost Particle
related.hook: Trillions of neutrinos stream through your body every second, yet they almost never touch anything. To catch even a few, physicists build some of the most audacious detectors ever conceived.

related.title: How Many Elementary Particles Are There, Really?
related.hook: Count the Standard Model's particles and you might say 17 — but tweak the rules and the tally climbs past 900, with one rigorous answer that isn't even a whole number.

related.title: Antimatter
related.hook: Every particle has a mirror twin with opposite charge, and when the two meet they vanish in a flash of pure energy — yet the universe is almost entirely matter, and nobody fully knows why.

flashcards.prompt: Why do physicists keep looking for proton decay?
flashcards.back_html: Grand unified theories predict protons eventually decay. Detecting it would be direct evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model; failing to see it rules out models.

flashcards.prompt: What limits how sensitive a proton decay search can be?

choices.text: The exposure — detector mass times observation time — and the irreducible atmospheric neutrino background
The energy of the accelerator producing the protons
The temperature of the water in the tank

flashcards.explanation_html: Because the rate per proton is minuscule, you need enormous numbers of protons watched for years, and you must separate any candidate from atmospheric neutrino interactions.

flashcards.prompt: What was unusual about the decay channel searched here?
flashcards.back_html: The final state was a single charged antilepton plus X, an invisible massless neutral particle — so most of the signature has to be reconstructed from the lepton alone.
